_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 580 words, six questions in text order). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page and by Full test 1.
title: Time on her hands
subtitle: At twenty-four, Nadia Kerr is one of the youngest qualified clock restorers in the country. Tom Hale spent a day in her workshop.

cards.text: The workshop is above a bakery, and the first thing you notice is not the sound of ticking but the smell of bread. Nadia Kerr apologises for it as she lets me in, although I suspect she has made this joke before. 'People expect it to be silent and dusty up here,' she says, 'like a museum. Then they walk in and get hungry.' The room itself is small and very bright. Clocks hang on every wall, but only three of them are running. The rest, she explains, are waiting for her, some of them for more than a year.
cards.question: What does the writer suggest about Nadia's comment on the smell of bread?
choices: It embarrasses her more than she admits.
She has probably said it to other visitors.
She would prefer to work somewhere quieter.
It explains why so few clocks are running.
cards.highlight: I suspect she has made this joke before
cards.why: 'I suspect she has made this joke before': the writer thinks she says it to everyone who visits.

cards.text: Nadia did not set out to mend clocks. At school she was, in her own words, 'the person who took things apart and lost the screws'. She started a degree in engineering, found the lectures dull, and left after a term without any clear idea of what she would do instead. It was her grandmother who suggested she visit Arthur Penn, an elderly clockmaker who had repaired the family's carriage clock for decades. 'I think she just wanted me out of the house,' Nadia says, laughing. 'She certainly didn't imagine I'd stay for six years.'
cards.question: Why did Nadia leave university?
choices: She had already decided to become a clockmaker.
Her grandmother persuaded her to leave.
She did not find the course interesting.
She failed her exams at the end of the first term.
cards.highlight: found the lectures dull, and left after a term without any clear idea of what she would do instead
cards.why: She 'found the lectures dull' and left 'without any clear idea of what she would do instead', so she had not yet chosen clocks.

cards.text: Penn took her on as an apprentice, although at first he gave her nothing more demanding than cleaning tiny brass wheels. For months she was not allowed to touch a working clock. Nadia admits she found this frustrating at the time, and nearly gave up on several occasions. Looking back, however, she believes it was the most valuable part of her training. 'Cleaning teaches you to look,' she says. 'By the time he let me near a real repair, I knew what every part was for and, more importantly, what it looked like when it was worn.'
cards.question: How does Nadia now feel about the first months of her apprenticeship?
choices: She regrets that she nearly gave up.
She thinks Penn was too strict with her.
She sees them as an essential stage of her training.
She wishes she had been given real repairs sooner.
cards.highlight: Looking back, however, she believes it was the most valuable part of her training
cards.why: 'Looking back, however, she believes it was the most valuable part of her training.' The frustration was at the time, not now.

cards.text: Penn retired three years ago and left her the business, along with a long list of customers who were not entirely convinced that a young woman could be trusted with their family treasures. One man arrived, saw her at the workbench and asked when 'the clockmaker' would be back. Nadia did not argue. She simply told him to leave the clock and return in a week. 'When he came back it was working perfectly. He didn't say much, but he's brought me four more since then.'
cards.question: What does the story about the male customer show about Nadia?
choices: She let the quality of her work answer his doubts.
She was upset by his attitude but hid her feelings.
She felt she had to explain her qualifications to him.
She was surprised when he brought her more clocks.
cards.highlight: Nadia did not argue. She simply told him to leave the clock and return in a week
cards.why: 'Nadia did not argue. She simply told him to leave the clock' and the perfect repair changed his mind.

cards.text: What surprises most visitors is how little of her job involves actually fixing things. Much of her time is spent deciding what not to do. A modern repairer, she explains, could replace a worn part in minutes, and the clock would keep better time than ever. But it would no longer be the same object. 'Somebody made every piece of this by hand, two hundred years ago,' she says, turning a small wheel towards the light. 'If I throw that away, I've thrown away the only thing that makes it worth repairing.'
cards.question: Why does Nadia avoid replacing worn parts?
choices: New parts would make the clocks less accurate.
Her customers cannot afford modern parts.
It takes longer than repairing the original ones.
The original parts are what give a clock its value.
cards.highlight: If I throw that away, I've thrown away the only thing that makes it worth repairing
cards.why: 'If I throw that away, I've thrown away the only thing that makes it worth repairing.' A new part would actually keep better time.

cards.text: This attitude does not always make business sense. Nadia charges far less than the hours she spends would justify, and she turns down work she considers unnecessary, such as polishing old cases until they look new. When I suggest that she could earn more by being less particular, she shrugs. 'Probably. But then I'd be doing a different job, and I'd be bored by Christmas.' As I leave, one of the three running clocks strikes four, slightly ahead of the others. Nadia glances at it and makes a note. It will be weeks before it goes back to its owner, and she seems in no hurry at all.
cards.question: What does the end of the article suggest about Nadia?
choices: She is annoyed when a clock does not keep time.
She is happy to work at her own pace.
She is worried about returning clocks late.
She is too busy to spend long with visitors.
cards.highlight: she seems in no hurry at all
cards.why: The clock will take weeks yet 'she seems in no hurry at all'. She only makes a note, so she is not annoyed.
